fn productExceptSelf(nums: list[int]) list[int]:
    res = list(nums.size, 1)

    prod = 1
    for i, num in nums:
        res[i] = prod
        prod *= num

    prod = 1
    for i, num in reverse nums:
        res[i] *= prod
        prod *= num

    return res

After the include branch, pop removes exactly the element pushed at this level. The exclude branch then sees the original subset. This is ordinary backtracking with explicit push, recurse, and undo steps; no additional control-flow feature is needed.

Fixtures compare results as unordered groups, allowing any subset order or element order while preserving duplicates for comparison. Missing subsets, repeated subsets, or repeated elements remain failures. Cases include empty input, zero, negative and unsorted values, and exact large integers.

For n elements there are 2^n results containing n * 2^(n - 1) integers when n is positive. Time and output storage are O(n * 2^n), with O(n) auxiliary space for the current subset and recursion stack. Empty input takes constant work and storage. The input list is not modified.
examples.birdie:
fn subsets(nums: list[int]) list[list[int]]:
    res = []
    subset = []

    fn dfs(i: int):
        if i >= nums.size:
            res.push(subset.copy())
            return

        subset.push(nums[i])
        dfs(i + 1)

        subset.pop()
        dfs(i + 1)

    dfs(0)
    return res
examples.python:
class Solution:
    def subsets(self, nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
        res = []
        subset = []

        def dfs(i: int) -> None:
            if i >= len(nums):
                res.append(subset.copy())
                return

            subset.append(nums[i])
            dfs(i + 1)

            subset.pop()
            dfs(i + 1)

        dfs(0)
        return res

examples.title: Subtree of Another Tree
examples.description: At each node, compare the entire subtree with the candidate. If it does not match, search the left and right subtrees.
examples.note: A match requires identical values and shape, including every descendant. LeetCode supplies nonempty input trees; the recursive search can still reach an empty root.
notes: The root == none guard ends the search at an empty subtree. It narrows root to TreeNode in the remaining body, so root.left and root.right are safe to read.

or tries the current position, then the left subtree, then the right subtree, stopping at the first successful match. A failed comparison at one position does not prevent finding a match deeper in that subtree.

sameTree captures no state, so it is a separate helper below isSubtree in both versions. Each problem is standalone: the helper is included here rather than depending on the separate Same Tree example.
The comparison helper uses the same guard order as Same Tree. It matches two absent nodes, rejects one absent node or different values, then checks corresponding children with short-circuit and.
An empty subRoot is outside LeetCode's input contract. The supplied algorithm returns false in that case; this translation preserves that behavior rather than treating an empty candidate as a match.

For m nodes in root and n nodes in subRoot, the worst-case time is O(m * n) under the usual unit-cost assumptions. The nested search and comparison follow paths inside root, using O(h) recursion space for root height h. Neither input tree is modified.

examples.title: Top K Frequent Elements
examples.description: Count each value, group values into frequency buckets, then collect the k most frequent values from the highest buckets.
examples.note: Assume 1 <= k <= the number of distinct input values. The frequency of any value is at most nums.size, so nums.size + 1 buckets cover every possible frequency.
notes: list(nums.size + 1, list) calls the list factory separately for each bucket. The type list[list[int]] is inferred from the values pushed into those buckets.
counter(nums) produces counter[int]. The key/count loop visits distinct numbers in first-appearance order; values with the same frequency enter their bucket in that order.
reverse buckets visits frequencies from highest to lowest without creating a reversed list. extend appends every value from the current bucket in its existing order.
res[:k] allocates a shallow copy of the first k elements. The size check ensures the prefix is in bounds and limits the result to exactly k values.
With the stated k constraint, the loop returns before the final fallback. The final return keeps a list result explicit on every path.
Under the usual constant-cost hashing, equality, and integer-operation assumptions, the bucket algorithm takes expected O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space. It does not sort the input or mutate it.

examples.title: Two Sum
examples.concept: Find a pair with a map.
examples.description: For each number, look up its complement among earlier numbers. Return their indices when a pair is found.
examples.note: Parameter types are explicit. The map’s key and value types are inferred from how it is used.
notes: Check the map before inserting the current value so the same element is not used twice.
The function returns the two indices when it finds a pair, or an empty list when no pair exists.

Valid Anagram
examples.description: Count character differences in a 26-slot list. Equal lengths and zero final counts mean the strings are anagrams.
examples.note: The input is assumed to contain only lowercase English letters a–z. Subtracting 'a' from a character maps it to an index from 0 through 25.
notes: list(26, 0) creates 26 initialized integer slots. This keeps the fixed-alphabet representation from the Python solution and avoids hash-table operations.

Subtracting two characters returns the difference of their Unicode scalar values as an int. c1 - 'a' gives the slot for a lowercase English letter. The .code property remains available for raw scalar values; this indexing scheme is not a general Unicode anagram algorithm.

Each zipped pair increments the count for the first string and decrements the count for the second. Birdie’s zip requires equal lengths; the early size check returns false before a mismatch could raise an error.
all(v == 0 for v in freqs) checks counts lazily and stops at the first nonzero value. It does not allocate an intermediate list of booleans.
In the usual unit-cost model, the algorithm takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space using 26 counter slots. Birdie’s arbitrary-precision integer operations still depend on operand size.

The draft counter API also permits counter(s) == counter(t), comparing character frequencies independently of insertion order. This example keeps the explicit array-based algorithm as its primary solution.

examples.title: Valid Parentheses
examples.description: Push opening brackets. For each closing bracket, pop and check the matching opener.
examples.note: The stack stores char values. Its element type is inferred from the values pushed onto it.
notes: Reject a closing bracket if the stack is empty or the brackets disagree.
The input is assumed to contain only ()[]{} characters. At the end, an empty stack means all brackets were matched. Birdie uses a dedicated stack type; Python uses a list with append and pop.

examples.title: Valid Sudoku
examples.description: Check each row, column, and 3×3 square for repeated digits, ignoring empty cells.
examples.note: Assume a 9×9 board containing digits 1–9 or '.'. Validity concerns the filled cells; it does not require a completed or solvable board.
notes: Birdie represents each cell as char. Python represents the same cells as one-character strings. Both examples use the same helper, extracted variables, and check order, with the main algorithm first and validGroup below it.

validGroup captures no enclosing variables, so it is a separate function. Birdie registers function declarations before ordinary execution, allowing the main function to call a helper written later. The Python helper is also top-level and is defined before the judge invokes the main method.
for i until 9 starts at zero and excludes nine. Adding step 3 visits square origins 0, 3, and 6. Nonzero starts remain explicit in the square comprehension.
List comprehensions eagerly collect a column or square. Multiple for clauses run like nested loops and produce a flat list. Their bindings do not leak into the enclosing function.
Each call to validGroup creates a fresh set[char]. continue skips empty cells, and the first repeated digit makes the group invalid. None of the checks modifies the input board.
Each of the 81 cells is examined in its row, column, and square unless validation returns early. Work and auxiliary storage are bounded for the fixed 9×9 board.

examples.title: Validate Binary Search Tree
examples.description: Validate every node against the strict lower and upper bounds inherited from its ancestors.
examples.note: Start with infinite bounds, then tighten the appropriate bound when descending into each subtree.
notes: The helper's number bounds accept exact integers and the built-in -inf and inf values. Node values stay finite integers. Python imports inf from math and uses int | float annotations because its infinity values are floats; it does not convert integer node values to floats.
An absent node is a valid empty subtree, so the helper returns true immediately. An empty input tree is valid too.

The chained comparison min_val < node.val < max_val enforces strict ordering, rejects duplicates, and checks inherited ancestor bounds. Each operand is evaluated at most once, and a failed comparison skips the rest of the chain.

The recursive and visits the right subtree first and skips the left subtree when the right subtree is invalid. This preserves the original traversal order while avoiding the eager evaluation caused by separate right and left assignments.
dfs captures no state and is a separate helper below isValidBST in both versions. LeetCode supplies TreeNode; the record declaration shows its standalone Birdie form.

Shared cases include distinct integers above floating-point precision and beyond machine integer ranges to check exact ordering. The initial infinities do not impose a finite maximum or minimum integer value.
Worst-case time is O(n), with O(h) recursion space for tree height h. Invalid subtrees can end the traversal early. The tree is not modified.

examples.title: Word Search II
examples.description: Find dictionary words formed by orthogonally adjacent board cells, without reusing a cell in a word.
examples.note: Build a trie, backtrack through matching paths, and prune branches after their remaining words are found.
notes: TrieNode is part of this solution, not a supplied type. Its optional word field stores a complete word at terminal nodes. map(TrieNode) supplies fresh children during dictionary construction; all DFS child reads are guarded by membership checks and do not create paths.

The board is a nonempty rectangular list of character rows, matching the character representation in Valid Sudoku. Words are nonempty and the visited marker # is excluded from the board and dictionary alphabet. JSON fixtures transport each character as a one-scalar string.

The nested dfs procedure captures the board, result list, dimensions, and direction list. It mutates collections and record fields without rebinding captured names, so no outer entries are required. The four directions are allocated once, outside recursion, in both languages.

When a word is found, clearing node.word prevents duplicate output from another path or start cell. The optional field's presence check is explicit; map emptiness still uses not node.chars. The fixtures compare results as an unordered multiset, so duplicate output remains an error.

Each DFS call marks its cell, explores eligible neighbors, and restores the original character before pruning. A branch is removed only when it has neither child paths nor an unreported terminal word. remove(char) removes the map entry; other references to that node retain ordinary reference semantics. Python uses del for the known-present key.

Pruning does not remove from a collection being iterated: traversal uses the separate direction list. Finding a shorter prefix word must not remove a branch needed by a longer word. Failed branches must restore cells before another branch or starting position explores them.

For total dictionary length S, R rows, C columns, and maximum word length L, construction takes expected O(S) work. A loose search upper bound is O(R * C * 4^L); trie rejection and pruning often reduce it substantially. Trie storage is O(S), recursion depth is at most min(L, R * C), and the output list is additional. The input board is restored on normal completion.
